messages.author: 06064714ad065b9b
messages.subject: Question about identified model
parts:
Hi, 

I am using SEM to work with fMRI data and encountered some problem:

Here are my codes:

model.SPE <- '
  # latent variables
  F =~ F1 + F2 + F3 + F4 + F5
  E =~ E1
  P =~ P1 + P2
 
  F ~ E + P
  P ~ F + E
  E ~ F + P'

model.EST <- sem(model.SPE, data = response_scale,
                 group = "tasktype")

And this is the warning message:

Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.

The I changed the estimating method:

model.EST <- sem(model.SPE, data = response_scale,
                 group = "tasktype", estimator = "MLR")

The warning message changed to:

The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
    (= -2.717168e-05) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that
    the model is not identified.

And the se of my parameters is large. I suspected that my model was not identified. However, I was in lack of the knowledge to design an identified model to answer my research question: what is the reciprocal relationship between the three brain areas.

It's also helpful to tell me what is an identified model~

Thanks for helping!

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Question about identified model
parts:
Yes, the structural model that you describe is fundamentally not identified. Each structural variable (your F, E and P) needs its own predictor not shared with the other structural variables. The observed variable indicators (F1, F2 and so forth) do not count. There is no way to resolve this without the additional predictors.
You can see the problem by looking at the covariance matrix of the structural variables:
     F   P   E
F   x
P   x    x
E   x    x   x
Currently, you are trying to estimate 6 structural paths from the 6 unique elements of this covariance matrix, but you also have to estimate 3 residual variances for the 3 structural variables. That is estimating 9 unknowns from the 6 knowns--if we treat this covariance matrix itself as known. The algebra for obtaining unique solutions for model parameters will not work without additional predictors for F, P and E.
--Ed Rigdon
